strengths: Theoretically sound twisted SMC framework with rigorous mathematical derivations and asymptotic consistency

Creative technical solutions to discrete gradient computation: first-order Taylor approximation is practical and empirically validated; continuous reformulation of denoising model handles carry-over unmasking constraint
Well-motivated training-free approach that avoids fine-tuning and reward over-optimization
Comprehensive technical exposition with clear algorithm, gradient analysis, and connections to continuous-time SMC
Convincing empirical evidence that first-order approximation achieves near-optimal performance (rewards, EMD, diversity) compared to exact locally optimal proposal
weaknesses: Experiments limited to toy datasets only (2D Gaussians and 28×28 binarized MNIST): no validation on the motivating applications mentioned in introduction (molecular generation, protein design, math reasoning), severely limiting evidence of practical utility

Severely insufficient baseline comparisons: only compared against 'approximate guidance'; missing comparisons with RL fine-tuning methods (Wang et al. 2024), classifier-based/free guidance variants (Schiff et al. 2024), and concurrent SMC work (Lee et al. 2025) mentioned in related work

Critical practical limitation with standard masked diffusion models: unmasked pixels cannot be modified, making guidance ineffective in later timesteps; workaround requires ReMDM/UDLM instead of standard masked diffusion, limiting applicability to currently popular methods

Temperature schedule λ_t requires manual hand-crafting with no principled selection method; different schedules needed for different models (Figure 6); paper states 'we needed to carefully choose the tempering schedule' suggesting brittleness and difficulty in applying to new problems

No computational cost analysis or scalability evaluation: uses different particle counts (2000 vs 20), unclear how this affects results and computational efficiency; no comparison of computational complexity versus baselines
Approximation quality concerns: Figure 1 shows first-order Taylor approximation has EMD 1.72 vs 1.14 for exact proposal; no theoretical bounds on approximation error or guidance on when it fails

Inconsistency between theory and practice: gradient analysis (Appendix D) uses modified formulation (Eq. 37) but experiments use original formulation (Eq. 16) with 'slightly different gradients'; this discrepancy undermines the gradient analysis

Incomplete experimental evaluation: missing confidence intervals, error bars, statistical significance testing; sensitivity analysis absent for key hyperparameters (particle count, ESS threshold, temperature schedule); reward estimation uses different sample counts (100 vs 1) without justification

strengths: Technically sound core contribution: first-order Taylor approximation of locally optimal SMC proposal is principled and well-executed
Strong theoretical grounding with thorough connection to continuous-time SMC formulations in appendix
Clear problem motivation addressing real limitations of existing alignment methods (over/under-optimization)
Clever handling of discrete gradient issues through Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and continuous reformulation of denoising model
Good experimental validation within scope with clear metrics and oracle comparisons on synthetic tasks
Honest discussion of limitations and challenges with different diffusion model types
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only toy problems (mixture-of-Gaussians and binarized MNIST) evaluated; motivating applications (molecular generation, protein design, math reasoning) never demonstrated
Method struggles fundamentally with masked diffusion models, requiring careful per-task tempering schedule tuning, undermining claims of general applicability

Extensive hyperparameter tuning required (temperature schedule, ESS threshold, particle count, resampling fraction) contradicts 'training-free' positioning; no less burdensome than fine-tuning in practice

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only approximate guidance evaluated empirically; many related methods listed in Appendix E but none compared; concurrent work Lee et al. (2025) with similar SMC approach not empirically evaluated

No scalability analysis: computational cost not discussed, no runtime comparisons, dramatic particle count variation (2000 vs 20) not justified, practical feasibility for high-dimensional problems unclear
First-order Taylor approximation quality not analyzed: no error bounds, no analysis of approximation error's impact on importance weight variance
Missing ablation studies on key design choices: particle count, ESS threshold, reward estimation sample size, temperature schedule effects
Asymptotic unbiasedness claim in abstract not formally proven; proof or clear statement of assumptions needed

strengths: Solid theoretical framework with clear characterization of tractable importance weights and well-motivated propositions connecting optimal proposals to variance minimization
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (synthetic, language modeling, biology design, text-to-image) with consistent improvements and thorough ablations
Novel learned proposal approach via log-variance minimization (Equation 10) that is theoretically justified and practically motivated
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, algorithmic detail, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Practical solutions to real implementation challenges including low-confidence sampling and handling rewards defined only on clean data
Systematic investigation of proposal choice impact, demonstrating that better proposal approximations consistently improve SMC performance
weaknesses: Limited core novelty given very recent concurrent work (Singhal et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025, Holderrieth et al. 2025) already applying SMC to discrete diffusion; main contribution (log-variance minimization for learning proposals) is somewhat incremental

Insufficient analysis of approximation errors, particularly for product targets (Eq. 6) where detailed balance introduces unavoidable error; no characterization of approximation quality or impact on performance
Lack of practical guidance: hyperparameters vary significantly across tasks (Table 3) but no principled approach for selection on new problems; unclear when to use SMCbase/SMCgrad/SMCamot variants
Computational cost analysis entirely absent despite linear scaling with particle count; no wall-clock time comparisons or cost-benefit analysis provided, making practical deployment guidance unclear
Evidence of reward over-optimization: language modeling (Table 1) shows 100% toxicity but increased PPL and decreased diversity; claims about avoiding over-optimization via SMC lack strong support

Complexity of amortised proposal training underspecified: reference distribution choice (q_ref), additional hyperparameter tuning, and task-dependent settings add implementation burden not fully discussed
